title: Coaching Cut 51: Over-modelling
author: Cognitive Coaching
summary: This entry in the Cognitive Coaching 'Coaching Cuts' series identifies over-modelling as a specific coaching pitfall: the coach models not just the targeted action step but also what comes before or after it, diluting the coachee's focus and making it unclear what they are meant to practise. The article explains why the pitfall is so natural — the surrounding lesson context feels logical to include — and how it backfires: when a more complex adjacent skill (like responding to mini-whiteboard errors) is modelled alongside a simpler procedural one (a whiteboard routine), the complex skill captures more attention even though it is not the target. The fix is deliberate isolation: tell the coachee exactly where the model starts and stops, accept that the cut-off will feel unnatural, and trust that the boundary communicates the value of the skill being practised.
points: Over-modelling happens because the bits around the action step feel natural to include — the coach mentally inhabits a real lesson flow and lets the model spill beyond its intended boundaries.

When a more cognitively demanding adjacent skill is modelled alongside the target skill, it captures disproportionate attention, making the simpler target look like a preamble rather than the actual focus.
The result is a coachee who is unsure what they are rehearsing; a coachee without clarity about the action step will treat a manageable target as overwhelming.
The fix requires deliberate verbal framing: the coach announces exactly where the model begins and ends before demonstrating, giving the coachee a defined object of attention.
An abrupt stop at the boundary actually communicates something important: that this routine is worth getting right on its own terms, not just as a lead-in to more interesting content.
quotes: The pitfall lives in the modelling stage of coaching. The coach stands up, models the action step, and the coachee watches. So far so good. But the coach doesn't stop at the action step. They keep going, modelling what comes next, or what came before, or both. By the time they finish, the coachee has seen a longer sequence of teaching and can't tell where the action step started and stopped.

Over-modelling doesn't happen because coaches are careless. It happens because the bits around the action step feel natural to include. If the action step is about developing a whiteboard routine, it feels logical to also show what you'd do once the boards are up.

The problem is that coaching isn't a real lesson. The model exists to give the coachee a clear, focused image of the thing they are working on. The moment you extend beyond the action step, you dilute that focus.

If you don't have that clarity, what should be a manageable step soon feels like too much. The coachee is now trying to hold two (or three) techniques at once, and the one they're meant to be practising gets lost in the noise.

By isolating the routine, you let the coachee see it clearly, understand why each part matters, and rehearse it without the cognitive load of also thinking about what comes next. The boundary also communicates something important: that this routine is worth getting right on its own.
